summary: This informational RFC defines a data format for shared brotli compression, adding shared dictionaries, large window support, and a container format to brotli (RFC 7932). These give significant compression gains.

eli5.summary: If both sides already hold the same cheat sheet, messages can be much shorter. This adds that cheat sheet idea to brotli compression.

questions: how does a brotli shared dictionary work
what is the shared brotli framing format
subtitle: Brotli compression extended with shared dictionaries, a huge sliding window and a container format.

tldr.problem: Regular brotli compresses each stream on its own, so it cannot take advantage of data the sender and receiver already share, and its window limits back references to a maximum of 24 bits.
tldr.mechanism: Shared brotli adds shared dictionaries (LZ77 dictionaries and custom static dictionaries), a large window mode with WBITS up to 62, and a framing format that stores multiple resources and refers to dictionaries.
tldr.outcome: Shared dictionaries and large window support allow significant compression gains over regular brotli. The RFC updates RFC 7932 and is backwards compatible with it.

today: RFC 9841 is an Informational document that updates RFC 7932 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It is the authoritative specification of the shared brotli formats.

sections.title: What Shared Brotli Adds
sections.content:
This RFC extends the brotli compressed data format of RFC 7932 with three abilities. Shared dictionaries give the encoder and decoder a static shared context. Large window brotli allows much larger back-reference distances, which helps files over 16 MiB. The framing format is a container that stores multiple resources and can reference dictionaries.

The document is the authoritative specification of the shared brotli data formats and of the backwards-compatible changes to brotli. It defines the serialized dictionary format, the framing format, the encoding of window bits and distances for large window brotli, and the encoding of shared dictionary references. It is aimed at implementers who compress or decompress the format; familiarity with LZ77 coding helps but is not required.

Multi-byte numbers are unsigned and stored least significant byte first, and data elements are packed into bytes starting with the least significant bit, with prefix codes packed starting with their most significant bit.
sections.eli5: Shared brotli gives the squishing method three new tricks: a shared cheat sheet, a much longer memory for repeats, and a box that holds many squished files together.

sections.title: Shared Dictionaries
sections.content:
A shared dictionary is data known to both compressor and decompressor, and both MUST use exactly the same one. It is especially useful for short inputs. If no shared dictionary is set, the decoder behaves as in RFC 7932. There are two ways to share context.

  • LZ77 dictionary: a sequence of bytes that references can point into, as if the bytes sat just outside the regular window. Multiple LZ77 dictionaries can be set.
  • Custom static dictionary: a word list with transforms that replaces the built-in static dictionary data of RFC 7932 (Appendices A and B). It can be switched based on the literal context, and can include a reference to the original dictionary.

A transform is a possible prefix, an operation, a parameter for some operations, and a possible suffix. Operations 0 to 20 are those of RFC 7932 (Identity, OmitLast1 to 9, FermentFirst, FermentAll, OmitFirst1 to 9). Two new ones, ShiftFirst (21) and ShiftAll (22), shift specially encoded scalar values by a parameter.
sections.eli5: A dictionary here is a shared notebook of useful words and phrases. Because both sides have the same notebook, a short pointer can stand for a long phrase.

sections.title: The Shared Dictionary Stream
sections.content:
A serialized dictionary starts with a 2-byte file signature (bytes 91 and 0). Next comes a varint, LZ77_DICTIONARY_LENGTH, and that many bytes of LZ77 dictionary. A varint is base 128: each byte contributes seven bits, the last byte has its top bit 0, and the stream is invalid if the 9th byte is present with its top bit set.

Then follow NUM_CUSTOM_WORD_LISTS (0 to 64) word lists, each described by 28 bytes of SIZE_BITS_BY_LENGTH for word lengths 4 to 31 and then the word data, and NUM_CUSTOM_TRANSFORM_LISTS (0 to 64) transform lists made of prefix/suffix strings and transform triplets. If any custom list exists, NUM_DICTIONARIES (1 to 64) pairs a word list with a transform list, with an optional 64-entry CONTEXT_MAP choosing which dictionary applies for each of the 64 literal contexts.
sections.eli5: This is the label on the notebook: how long it is, which word lists it holds, and which rules to bend the words with.

sections.title: Large Window Brotli
sections.content:
Large window brotli allows a sliding window beyond the 24-bit maximum of regular brotli. The stream stays backwards compatible, with optional differences. The stream header gets a new 14-bit pattern: 8 bits with the value 00010001 to signal a large window stream, then 6 bits of WBITS in the range 10 to 62.

The distance alphabet also grows: the maximum number of extra bits is 62, and the theoretical largest size is 16 + NDIRECT + (124 << NPOSTFIX). Distances may not exceed (1 << 63) - 4. A decoder without 64-bit integer support may reject streams with WBITS above 30 or a distance symbol able to encode a distance larger than 2147483644.

A shared brotli compressed stream without the framing format may use LZ77 dictionaries, custom static dictionaries, and either regular or large window brotli.
sections.eli5: Regular brotli can only look back so far to spot repeats. Large window brotli lets it look back across a gigantic file.

sections.title: The Framing Format
sections.content:
A framing format stream begins with a 4-byte signature (0x91 0x0a 0x42 0x52) whose first byte is an invalid WBITS combination for brotli. A container flags byte follows; bits 0 and 1 are a version that MUST be 00, and bit 2 chooses between a simple single-resource file with no final footer and a full container that may hold several resources, metadata and a central directory and MUST end with a final footer. After that come chunks.

Each chunk has a varint length, a chunk type byte (0 to 10) and, for most types, a codec byte: uncompressed, keep decoder, brotli or shared brotli. A shared brotli chunk lists dictionary references, at most 1 serialized dictionary and 15 prefix dictionaries, which may point to an earlier chunk or name a dictionary by a 256-bit HighwayHash. Circular references are not allowed.

Metadata fields use a 2-letter code; unknown lowercase codes make the stream invalid, while uppercase codes are custom and can be ignored. A resource is one data chunk, or a first partial chunk, any middle partial chunks and a last partial chunk. The central directory and repeat metadata chunks allow finding and listing resources quickly.
sections.eli5: The framing format is a box with labelled compartments. Each compartment says what is inside, how it was squished, and which cheat sheet it needs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The considerations for RFC 7932 apply, plus the same care for decoding the new formats. A dictionary must be treated with the same precautions as the content, because changing it changes the decompressed result.

The CRIME attack shows it is a bad idea to compress data from mixed public and private sources, and that includes dictionaries. If an adversary controls part of the data and sees compressed sizes, the data can reveal the dictionary; if the adversary controls the dictionary, it can learn about the data. The most robust defence is not compressing private data such as cookies. Weaker ideas are randomising compression, and not using dictionaries for cross-domain requests. Dictionaries should be based on content you control or generic large-scale content, and updated at large intervals (days, not seconds).

HighwayHash identifiers do not guarantee against collisions in an adversarial environment, so such users should validate a negotiated dictionary with a cryptographically secure hash. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: If someone can sneak words into your shared notebook, they can learn your secrets from how short the messages get. So keep secrets out and control who writes in the notebook.
